questions.question: How do I know this relationship is actually becoming healthier over time, rather than merely becoming deeper, more intense, or more entangled?
questions.note: The article supplies many ingredients—honesty, trust, self-regulation, outside support, agape, community—but no explicit longitudinal success test.

questions.question: How do I distinguish a repairable trigger or growth edge from a fundamental incompatibility—or from a relationship that is simply unsafe?
questions.note: Danger receives a clear safety boundary, and incompatibility appears throughout, but the middle category—painful yet workable versus structurally wrong—remains distributed rather than resolved.

questions.question: After an ordinary fight, what does a successful repair actually look like?
questions.note: The article asks how a prospective partner repaired past conflicts and later offers several repair ingredients, but there is no compact ordinary-conflict repair sequence.

questions.question: How much mismatch can two people realistically work through before 'growth' becomes an excuse for incompatibility?
questions.note: The draft distinguishes complementarity, maturity gaps, sexual fit, values, and irreconcilable memories, but not a general decision rule—which may or may not be desirable.

questions.question: While I am inside the relationship, how can I tell durable romantic love from attachment, idealization, trauma activation, or simply wanting to be wanted?
questions.note: This distinction is central to several sections but remains a distributed argument rather than a reader-facing discriminant.

questions.question: Once children actually arrive, how do we keep the romantic relationship alive while parenting, rather than only planning for children or protecting them if we separate?
questions.note: Children are a recurring organizing test from the opening onward, but the dedicated Children section concentrates on obligations and breakup/co-parenting.

questions.question: Before merging lives, what should couples actually work out about money, labor, dependency, and household responsibility?
questions.note: The article repeatedly uses money, provision, work, housing, and resentment as examples but does not develop a practical treatment of shared logistics.

questions.question: What is the difference between a healthy boundary and an attempt to control or punish a partner?
questions.note: Boundaries, demands, consent, exclusivity, coercion, and safety all appear, but the distinction itself is not made explicit.

questions.question: If I do not already have a commune or shared community, what can I practically do now?
questions.note: The Two Pillars section answers this directly with mutual friendships, meetups, shared purpose, and partial community-building.

questions.question: What if we are already deeply entangled or married, so the advice to slow down comes too late?
questions.note: The article anticipates this question and immediately opens the next major section with it.

questions.question: What if sexual compatibility or libido changes after we are already bonded?
questions.note: The early sex section explicitly recommends discussing later divergence before either person is hurt; later material treats fit as partly discoverable only through experience.

questions.question: How do I avoid making my partner my entire emotional and social world?
questions.note: The article gives a dedicated section and later community treatment.

prefix_probes.live_question: If love needs both eros and agape, how do I know whether a specific person and I can actually build a life together?
If sex can bond me before I know the person well, how do I get close enough to learn who they are without being swept into a life bond?
Even if I screen carefully, what happens when intimacy activates wounds neither of us could see beforehand?
Where is the line between healthy complementarity and a mismatch that is too costly to keep working on?
What keeps an intense sacred bond from collapsing into a sealed two-person world?
What happens if the agreements remain but the feelings change—or one person no longer wants the same relationship?
What if we are already married, bonded, or in trouble, so prevention advice arrives too late?
